analysis.one_liner: Requires large automakers to sell at least 20,000 new vehicles a year equipped with drunk-driving prevention technology.
analysis.headline: Introduced December 18, 2025 with no cosponsors and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it has not advanced.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require any automaker that sold more than 250,000 vehicles in a recent year to sell or import at least 10,000 vehicles a year meeting the federal 'DADSS' performance specs for detecting drunk driving, plus another 10,000 a year meeting Europe's newest crash-and-safety testing standard, which includes alcohol detection requirements. These minimums would stay in place only until the federal rule required by the 2021 infrastructure law takes effect, meaning the bill acts as a bridge to push the technology into showrooms sooner. Automakers that fail to meet the minimums would face civil penalties.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers, passengers, and pedestrians on roads where drunk driving remains a leading cause of traffic deaths. The bill targets roughly 13,000 U.S. deaths a year that involve alcohol-impaired driving by forcing a minimum volume of vehicles with impairment-detection technology into the market before the pending federal rule does so.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Road users and families of crash victims

how_it_helps.text: Requires large manufacturers to sell or import at least 10,000 vehicles per year that meet the DADSS (Driver Alcohol Detection System for Safety) performance specifications, technology designed to passively detect when a driver is over the alcohol limit. [S2]

Requires another 10,000 vehicles per year meeting Euro NCAP version 10.3, the European new-car safety standard published in December 2023, and automatically updates to stricter future versions of that standard unless federal regulators formally find a revision does not meet safety needs. [S2]
Attaches the bill's existing civil penalty structure to the new requirement, so a manufacturer that fails to meet the minimum volumes can be fined. [S2]

Expiring once the rule required by Section 24220 of the 2021 Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act takes effect, meaning the mandate is designed to fill the gap until the government's own anti-drunk-driving rule is finished. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Large automakers, which must engineer, equip, and sell at least 20,000 vehicles a year with impairment-detection and enhanced-safety equipment regardless of market demand. Some of that cost could be passed to buyers of those specific vehicles, and consumers overall bear the residual risk if the technology adds cost or produces false warnings.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large automakers and possibly their buyers

drawbacks.text: The mandate is a quota, not a fleet-wide rule: it requires a minimum number of compliant vehicles rather than requiring all new cars to carry the technology, so most new vehicles sold in a year would still have no impairment detection. [S2]

It locks in specific technical standards by reference, including a European standard whose future revisions auto-apply unless the Transportation Secretary affirmatively overrides them after a rulemaking, limiting Congress's and regulators' flexibility. [S2]

Meeting the volume requirements imposes engineering and per-unit costs on large manufacturers that could be passed through to vehicle prices, without any offsetting relief for smaller manufacturers, who are exempt. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential upside is real: impairment-detection technology addresses one of the largest remaining causes of road deaths. But the design is blunt. A fixed quota of 20,000 vehicles a year, tied to standards written by a European testing body, is a modest, somewhat awkward step compared with the fleet-wide rule Congress already ordered in the 2021 infrastructure law; the bill mainly tries to speed that rule's arrival. The cost to automakers is likely small relative to fleet size, and the safety benefit, while real, is limited by the quota structure.

outcome.mechanism: It is two days old at the end of the House's first session: introduced by Rep. Dingell, referred to Energy and Commerce, and sitting there with no cosponsors and no scheduled action.

narrative.text: Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-MI) introduced the DRIVE to HALT Drunk Driving Act on December 18, 2025. [S1]
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce. [S4]
As of its introduction, the bill has no cosponsors. [S3]

The bill would require covered manufacturers (those selling more than 250,000 vehicles in the second most recent calendar year) to sell or import at least 10,000 vehicles a year meeting the DADSS impairment-detection specifications and 10,000 meeting Euro NCAP version 10.3, with the requirement expiring once the rule mandated by Section 24220 of the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act takes effect. [S2]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No outcome yet; the bill has only been referred to committee, so automakers are not yet under any obligation and the status quo on drunk-driving technology stands.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo; no action yet taken

for.name: Rep. Debbie Dingell
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 18, 2025, named for the Abbas family, a Michigan family killed by a wrong-way drunk driver in 2019.

sides.party_line_note: There are no cosponsors and no votes yet, so no partisan shape to the support or opposition can be read from the record.

industries.note: Large manufacturers (over 250,000 vehicles/year) must sell or import at least 20,000 vehicles annually with impairment-detection or enhanced-safety equipment, adding engineering and per-unit costs that could reach consumers. The mandate expires once the federal impairment-rule under the 2021 infrastructure law takes effect, limiting its duration.

industries.industry: Impairment-detection and vehicle safety technology suppliers
industries.note: The bill guarantees an annual buyer base for DADSS-style alcohol-detection systems and Euro NCAP-compliant safety equipment, creating demand before a federal rule would. Better-detection technology serves the same outcome road users want.

analysis.trajectory: With one sponsor, zero cosponsors, and a referral to Energy and Commerce at the very end of the first session, the bill faces the usual long odds: most single-sponsor bills referred to committee in the closing days of a session never get a hearing or a markup. Without visible bipartisan cosponsorship or movement from the committee chair, it is likely to remain idle and die at the end of the 119th Congress unless support builds quickly.
